record.paper_title: Chapter 15: Open Questions and Future Directions in Titan Science
record.original_question: Is Titan geotectonically active at the present day, including cryovolcanism or other crustal deformation, or are the observed mountains, ridges, faults, and candidate cryovolcanic features ancient and eroded; and can high-resolution global mapping, spectroscopy, temporal-change detection, and subsurface sounding determine whether Titan is currently active?

evidence.quote: 7) Is there active geotectonic activity on Titan at the present day?

However, the fact that these features mostly appear heavily eroded and there is no evidence of present-day changes makes the timing of their origin uncertain and leaves open the question of whether present day crustal activity is occurring (Solomonidou et al., 2013).

A mapping polar orbiter equipped with multi-spectral passive and active surface imaging capability, as well as the ability to conduct sub-surface sounding (e.g. ice-penetrating radar, IPR) would allow us to much more clearly discern whether Titan is an active world at the present day, or not.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Saturn's largest moon, Titan, exhibits surface features including mountains, ridges, faults, and candidate cryovolcanic edifices (such as putative domes, flows, and depressions interpreted as possible cryovolcanic constructs). Many of these features appear heavily eroded, and to date no unambiguous temporal changes attributable to internal activity have been documented. Determine whether Titan is geotectonically active at the present day — that is, whether ongoing cryovolcanism or other crustal deformation is currently occurring — or whether the observed tectonic and candidate cryovolcanic features are ancient and now inactive. In addressing this, specify what combination of high-resolution global surface mapping, multi-spectral passive and active imaging, temporal change-detection observations, and subsurface sounding (e.g., ice-penetrating radar) would be sufficient to discriminate between an actively deforming/cryovolcanic Titan and a tectonically quiescent one, and characterize the expected observational signatures distinguishing these two scenarios.
artifact.status_search_result: As of 2026, no published observations have unambiguously demonstrated present-day geotectonic activity or active cryovolcanism on Titan; candidate cryovolcanic features remain debated, and definitive resolution is expected to require future missions (such as Dragonfly) or a dedicated polar orbiter with subsurface sounding capability. The question is widely regarded as open in the planetary-science community.

status_evidence.title: Cryovolcanism on Titan: New results from Cassini RADAR and VIMS
status_evidence.snippet: Solomonidou et al. discuss candidate cryovolcanic features on Titan and emphasize that present-day activity remains unconfirmed.
status_evidence.claim: Present-day cryovolcanic activity on Titan has not been confirmed; candidate features are debated.

status_evidence.title: Dragonfly: A Rotorcraft Lander Mission to Titan
status_evidence.snippet: NASA's Dragonfly mission is planned to investigate Titan's surface composition and geology, including potential evidence of cryovolcanism, after arrival in the 2030s.
status_evidence.claim: Future missions are expected to test whether Titan is presently geologically active.
